n: Eliphaz, the oldest-sounding and most respected of Job’s three friends, begins his second speech. The friendly tone of his first speech (chapters 4–5) is gone.

f.g: From Teman in Edom, a region known for its wise men (Jeremiah 49:7).

n: Eliphaz mocks Job’s words as hot air. A truly wise man, he says, would not fill himself with empty talk like a stomach bloated with wind.

f.g: The scorching desert wind (the sirocco) — a picture of words that are hot, harsh, and useless.

n: He asks whether arguing with words that accomplish nothing is fitting for a wise man. To Eliphaz, Job’s complaints are not just wrong but pointless.

f.g: Speech that does no good to anyone.

n: Eliphaz claims Job’s complaints undermine reverence for God. If people talked like Job, he suggests, they would stop fearing God and stop praying.

f.g: Literally “diminish devotion” — you are weakening worship and meditation before God.

n: He argues that Job’s very words reveal hidden sin. The way Job speaks, Eliphaz says, is the clever, slippery speech of a guilty person.

f.g: Shrewd or cunning people; the same word describes the serpent in Genesis 3:1.

n: Eliphaz insists he doesn’t need to accuse Job — Job’s own mouth convicts him. It is a sharp turn from comforter to prosecutor.

f.w: thine own lips testify against thee

n: With sarcasm he asks whether Job thinks he is the first human ever born, older than the hills, and therefore wiser than everyone.

f.g: Language used of Wisdom herself in Proverbs — Eliphaz mocks Job for acting as if he were Wisdom personified.

n: Eliphaz asks whether Job has listened in on God’s private council and kept its wisdom to himself.

f.g: Hebrew sod — the intimate council of God. Compare Amos 3:7, where the Lord reveals his secret to his prophets.

n: He turns Job’s earlier words back on him (12:3; 13:2). Job claimed his friends knew nothing he did not; Eliphaz says the reverse.

f.w: What knowest thou, that we know not?

n: Eliphaz appeals to age and tradition: gray-haired elders, older even than Job’s father, stand on the friends’ side.

f.g: In the ancient Near East gray hair signaled wisdom and authority.

n: He asks whether Job thinks God’s comforts — perhaps meaning the friends’ gentle words — are too small for him. Eliphaz sees his own counsel as God’s consolation.

f.g: Probably Eliphaz’s own earlier, gentle speech, which he presents as comfort from God.

n: Eliphaz asks why Job lets his emotions run away with him and why his eyes flash with anger.

f.g: Probably “flash” — eyes blazing in anger or defiance.

n: The real problem, Eliphaz says, is that Job is turning his spirit against God and letting reckless words escape.

f.g: “Spirit” here can also mean anger or breath — Job is venting his rage at God.

n: Eliphaz repeats the main point of his night vision (4:17): no mortal can be truly clean or righteous before God.
If God cannot fully trust even his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure to him, mortals have no ground to claim innocence.

f.g: “Holy ones” — heavenly beings or angels, not human believers.

n: How much worse is a human being who gulps down sin as easily as drinking water. Eliphaz’s view of humanity is very dark.
Eliphaz announces a lesson from his own experience. Ironically, what follows assumes Job is the wicked man he describes.

f.g: Eliphaz relies on personal observation and tradition, not on revelation.

n: His teaching, he says, is ancient wisdom handed down from the fathers and openly passed on.
These ancestors received the land as theirs alone, with no foreigners to corrupt their teaching — so their tradition is pure.

f.g: No outsider — Eliphaz claims the wisdom is untainted by foreign ideas.

n: Eliphaz begins his portrait of the wicked: such a person lives in constant inner anguish, never knowing how many years he has left.

f.g: Writhes as in labor pains — continual torment.

n: Even in good times the wicked man hears frightening sounds. He expects disaster to strike at any moment.

f.g: A raider or plunderer; Job’s losses to raiders (1:15, 17) make this a pointed jab.

n: He has no hope of escaping his darkness and feels the sword waiting for him.

f.g: Marked out for violent death.

n: Eliphaz pictures him wandering in search of food, knowing that his day of ruin is close at hand.

f.g: A day of calamity and judgment.

n: Distress and anguish overwhelm him like a king charging into battle.

f.w: as a king ready to the battle
f.g: A powerful attacker prepared to strike.

n: The reason for his downfall: he has shaken his fist at God and tried to set himself up against the Almighty.

f.w: stretcheth out his hand against God
f.g: A gesture of defiance — perhaps meant to describe how Eliphaz sees Job’s protests.

n: The wicked man is pictured as a reckless warrior charging at God with head down behind a heavy shield.

f.g: The raised metal knobs on a shield (buckler = small shield).

n: His face and body are thick with fat — a picture of self-indulgent, arrogant prosperity that has made him callous.

f.g: Thick folds or rolls of fat.

n: In the end he lives among abandoned ruins, cities and homes soon to become heaps of rubble.

f.g: Destined to be piles of ruins.

n: His wealth will not last, and his possessions will not spread across the land.

f.g: Possibly “his holdings” or “his grain” — the meaning is uncertain.

n: He will never escape darkness. Like a tree scorched by fire, his branches wither, and God’s breath sweeps him away.

f.g: Probably God’s breath — a picture of divine judgment.

n: Eliphaz warns: whoever trusts in emptiness will be repaid with emptiness.

f.g: Emptiness, worthlessness — what has no substance.
Payment, reward.

n: His end will come before his time, and his branch will never be green again.
Like a vine dropping unripe grapes or an olive tree shedding blossoms, the wicked lose their fruit before it matures.

f.w: cast off his flower as the olive
f.g: Olive trees shed many blossoms; the image is of fruitfulness lost.

n: Communities of the godless will be left desolate, and fire will burn the homes of those who take bribes.

f.g: Hebrew ḥanef — the godless or profane.
Tents of those enriched by bribes — a hint at Job’s supposed corruption (compare 22:6-9).

n: Eliphaz ends with a birth image: the wicked conceive trouble and give birth to emptiness. He has described evil well but misjudged Job.
